title: Curriculum Design
summary: Learn to design and improve curricula: layers of curriculum, writing outcomes with Bloom's taxonomy, backward design and alignment, scope, sequence and time planning, balanced and weighted assessment, and relevance and review.
audience: Teachers, heads of department, trainers, curriculum developers and education students

body.p: A curriculum is the planned set of learning experiences, content, skills, values and assessments that learners go through. It answers four big questions: what should learners learn, why, how will they learn it, and how will we know they have learned it?

list: Intended curriculum: what official documents and syllabuses say should be learned.
Enacted (implemented) curriculum: what actually happens in classrooms.
Attained curriculum: what learners actually learn.
Hidden curriculum: unwritten lessons about values, behaviour and power, such as who gets to speak or which languages are respected.

body.p: Gaps between these layers are common. A syllabus may promote problem-solving while crowded timetables and exam pressure push teachers towards memorisation. Good curriculum work pays attention to all layers.

Many countries have reformed curricula towards competencies, such as Kenya's Competency-Based Curriculum, while others refine content-based frameworks, such as South Africa's CAPS. Teachers and schools still make many design decisions within national frameworks.

body.tip: Read your official syllabus closely; teachers often discover flexibility and priorities they had missed.

lessons.title: Aims, outcomes and levels of thinking

body.p: Clear outcomes say what learners will be able to do by the end of a unit or course. They guide teaching, activities and assessment.

list: Start with an action verb that can be observed: explain, calculate, compare, design, evaluate.
Avoid vague verbs such as "understand" or "know" on their own.
Include the content and, if useful, the conditions or standard.
Example: "Learners will calculate the area of rectangles and triangles in real contexts, such as planning a garden."
Remember: recall facts.
Understand: explain ideas.
Apply: use knowledge in new situations.
Analyse: break ideas down and find relationships.
Evaluate: judge and justify.
Create: produce something new.

body.p: A balanced curriculum includes outcomes at several levels, not only remembering. Higher levels build on lower ones: learners need knowledge to analyse and create.

body.tip: Check your outcomes: if every verb is "list" or "define", add some that ask learners to apply, analyse or create.

body.p: Backward design (associated with Wiggins and McTighe's "Understanding by Design") plans in three stages, starting from the end.

steps: Identify desired results: the key outcomes and big ideas learners should understand.
Determine acceptable evidence: decide how learners will show they have met the outcomes (tasks, projects, tests).
Plan learning experiences: choose activities and teaching that prepare learners for that evidence.

body.p: This avoids the common trap of planning enjoyable activities first and hoping they lead somewhere. For a unit on water, the big idea might be "clean water depends on how communities manage sources"; evidence could be a group plan to protect a local water source; learning activities would include testing water, interviewing community members and studying diseases spread by unsafe water.

Outcomes, teaching activities and assessment should all point in the same direction. If the outcome is "design an experiment", a multiple-choice test of definitions does not assess it; a practical design task does.

body.tip: Write the final assessment task before planning lessons; it sharpens what you teach.

body.p: Scope is what is covered; sequence is the order. Good sequencing moves from simple to complex, concrete to abstract and familiar to unfamiliar, and respects prerequisites (fractions before percentages).

In a spiral curriculum, important ideas return each year at greater depth: fractions with objects in early grades, operations with fractions later, then algebraic fractions. Revisiting builds deep understanding and memory.

Calculate time honestly. A subject with 4 periods of 40 minutes a week for 40 weeks has 4 x 40 x 40 = 6400 minutes, about 106.7 hours a year, before losses to tests, events and absences. A unit needing 12 periods uses 12 x 40 = 480 minutes, or 8 hours; check that all the units together fit. Over-full syllabuses push teachers to rush and learners to memorise.

list: Map units across the year, with time allocations.
Leave buffer time for revision and catching up.
Coordinate with other subjects to reinforce skills, such as graphs in science and maths at the same time.

body.tip: Cut or combine low-priority content before you cut practice time for essential skills.

body.p: Assessment shows whether outcomes are achieved and guides teaching. A curriculum should specify a balanced mix.

list: Formative assessment (for learning): quick checks, questioning, quizzes and feedback during learning.
Summative assessment (of learning): tests, projects and exams at the end of a unit or year.
Performance tasks: practical work, presentations and portfolios that assess skills directly.
Self- and peer-assessment: learners judge work against criteria, building independence.

body.p: Programmes often combine marks. If a course counts a test as 40%, a project as 30% and an exam as 30%, a learner scoring 70, 80 and 60 gets a final mark of 0.4 x 70 + 0.3 x 80 + 0.3 x 60 = 70. Weights should reflect the importance of the outcomes each assessment measures.
Rubrics describe levels of quality for each criterion, making marking fairer and showing learners what good work looks like.

body.tip: Share rubrics with learners before they start a task; it is one of the most effective ways to improve their work.

body.p: Curricula should prepare learners for their lives, communities and future work. Relevance increases motivation and understanding.

list: Use local examples, languages, histories, environments and livelihoods.
Include skills for life and work: critical thinking, communication, collaboration, digital and financial literacy.
Represent diverse people fairly in materials and examples.
Make content accessible to learners with different needs and backgrounds.

body.p: Collect evidence: assessment results, learner and teacher feedback, classroom observation, and what happens to learners afterwards. Ask whether outcomes are being met, whether time and resources are realistic, and whether some groups are being left behind. Use the findings to revise the curriculum in planned cycles.

body.tip: Ask learners what helped them learn and what felt irrelevant; their answers often show exactly where to improve.
